blocks.text: Now I shall prove without any difficulty that this, whatever it is, fits the letaa. 1. That this kind of lizard is similar to the stellio, or even a species of it, is suggested by the fact that the most ancient of the interpreters, the Greek, the Chaldee and the Roman, render it stellio. 2. That it clings to the ground is gathered from the name itself. For in Arabic the verb لطا [laṭā] lataa, or لطئ [laṭiʾa] latia, properly means to cling, not to anything at all, but to the ground. It is never taken otherwise. Hence Damir, in the chapter قبرة [qubbara] Kobbara, or On the Lark: It is its nature that noise does not frighten it; and sometimes it is crushed by a millstone, ولطي بالارض حتي يتجاوزها الحجر [wa-laṭiya bi-l-arḍ ḥattā yatajāwazahā al-ḥajar] and it clings to the ground until the stone has passed over it. And in the chapter عنكبوت [ʿankabūt], or On the Spider, فانا اراد صيد الذباب لطي بالارض [fa-nā arāda ṣayd al-dhubāb laṭiya bi-l-arḍ] And when it wants to hunt flies, it clings to the ground. Thus לטאה letaa, derived from it, properly signifies the animal that clings to the ground. This is what Giauhari and Damir note in the definition of the vvachara. 3. Finally, that the letaa is a venomous animal, and one to be guarded against above all, is taught by the enlarged Lamed at the beginning of the name. For it is not written לטאה, but לטאה. Hence Buxtorf in the Commentarius Masorethicus, ch. 14: The small Masora notes an enlarged La- [col. 1075] med in the word והלטאה, Levit. XI, 30, which some render lizard, others stellio. The enlarged letter indicates that among the other reptiles this reptile is to be guarded against most of all.

As for the rest, what this animal is called in Greek no one could easily say, unless one thinks it to be a species of salamander. For some of the ancients compare the salamander with the stellio, as similar to it, or even a species of it. Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 52: The salamander is an animal similar to the stellio. The Scholiast of Nicander on the Alexipharmaca: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα, εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra, eidos askalabōtou]. 2. The same animal is said to infect whatever it treads on. Pliny, in the place cited above: If it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison. Likewise: If a crust of bread is baked over wood or a foot touched by it, the poisoning is the same. To this belongs what the people of Narbonne keep saying, according to Gesner: If a Blanda (that is, a salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much that even hens feeding on it die. Accordingly الوحرة [al-waḥara] alvvachara, to which the Arabs attribute these same things, might seem to be the same as the salamander, except that the colour does not agree. For in the wachara it is red, in the salamander variegated. Therefore the wachara is another kind of Arabian lizard, unknown to us, yet similar in [II, 500] many respects to the stellio and the salamander. Hence it is that לטאה letaa, which we take to be the vvachara of the Arabs, is rendered ܣܡܢܕܪܐ salamandra by the Syriac, and stellio by most of the other ancients ^{(1)}.
